title: ‘Vexilla Regis’ praises the Cross apart from Christ, then prays: ‘O cross, hail, only hope… grant pardon to the guilty’
source_text: XXII. In hymno qui incipit, Vexilla Regis prodeunt, & qui decantari solet Sabbato ante Passionem, & solennibus aliis diebus, ornatur primo Crux variis Elogiis quibus a Christo distinguitur, & vocatur Arbor decora & fulgida, Ornata regis purpura, Electa digno stipite tam sancta membra tangere, Beata cujus brachiis secli pependit pretium. Deinde haec ad eam oratio concipitur, O crux ave spes unica, hoc Passionis tempore, Auge piis justitiam, Reisque dona veniam.
pass_a_gloss: In the hymn which begins, The banners of the King go forth, and which is accustomed to be sung on the Saturday before the Passion and on other solemn days, first the Cross is adorned with various elogies by which it is distinguished from Christ, and is called a tree decorous and shining, Ornamented with the purple of a king, Chosen from a worthy stock to touch such holy members, Blessed on whose arms the price of the age hung. Then this prayer is conceived toward it: O cross, hail, only hope, in this time of the Passion, Increase justice for the pious, and grant pardon to the guilty.
pass_b_english: The Passion hymn Vexilla Regis first praises the Cross as distinct from Christ, then prays to it as ‘only hope’ for justice and pardon.

lemmas.gloss: The banners of the King go forth

choices.why: Hymn rhetoric treats the cross as addressee apart from Christ.
